title: Levite Towns and Cities of Refuge
overview: The LORD sets out towns for the Levites and creates six safe cities where someone who killed by accident could escape revenge and get a fair hearing.

parts.label: Towns for the Levites (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: The Levites were the tribe set apart to serve at worship and received no territory of their own, so every tribe was to give them towns with grazing land around them, larger tribes giving more. The two measurements in verses 4 and 5 are hard to fit together, and scholars still debate exactly how the land was laid out.

parts.label: Six cities of refuge (vv. 9-15)
parts.note: In this culture the closest relative of someone killed, called the avenger of blood, was expected to kill the killer, often in the heat of grief before asking what really happened. Six of the Levite towns, three on each side of the Jordan River, became safe places where anyone who had killed someone, Israelite or foreigner, could flee and live until a fair hearing.

parts.label: What counts as murder (vv. 16-21)
parts.note: Killing someone with a weapon, out of hatred, or by lying in wait showed clear intent, and the law says the avenger was to put that person to death. The safe cities were never meant to shelter a deliberate killer.

parts.label: When a death was an accident (vv. 22-29)
parts.note: If no harm was intended, the community judged the case and sent the killer back to the city of refuge, to stay there until the high priest died and to lose all protection by leaving early. The text never explains why the high priest's death ended this exile.

parts.label: Witnesses, no payoffs, the land (vv. 30-34)
parts.note: A death sentence required more than one witness, and no payment could buy off a murderer or shorten an accidental killer's stay. Bloodshed was seen as staining the land where the LORD lived among the people, a stain that, the text says, only the killer's own death could remove.

disagreement: Christians differ on why the high priest's death set the accidental killer free: some see it as a kind of atonement, with the priest's death covering the blood that was shed, which they read as pointing to the death of Jesus, while others see it simply as a national turning point that worked like a general amnesty.
think: When someone causes a death by accident, what do you think justice owes both the grieving family and the person responsible?
